title: Git basics
note: Neutral learning topic for the preview harness: Git concepts with prerequisites, practice questions and model answers. No roles, employers or personal stories.

competencies.title: What a repository is
competencies.explain: A repository is a folder whose full history Git keeps in a hidden .git folder. Every saved state of the files is a commit, and the history is the chain of commits back to the first one.

competencies.title: Stage and commit changes
competencies.explain: Git records changes in two steps: git add puts chosen changes in the staging area, and git commit saves exactly what is staged with a message. Small commits with clear messages make history easy to read and undo.

competencies.title: Work on a branch
competencies.explain: A branch is a movable name that points at a commit. New commits move the current branch forward, so you can try an idea on its own branch without touching main.

competencies.title: Merge a branch back
competencies.explain: git merge joins another branch's commits into the current one. When both sides changed the same lines Git stops with a conflict: edit the file to the version you want, add it and commit.

competencies.title: Push and pull with a remote
competencies.explain: A remote such as origin is another copy of the repository, usually on a server. git push sends your commits there, git fetch downloads new commits, and git pull fetches and merges them into your branch.

competencies.title: Undo safely
competencies.explain: git restore throws away uncommitted edits to a file, git revert adds a new commit that undoes an old one, and git reset moves a branch. Prefer revert for anything already pushed, because it never rewrites shared history.

questions.text: What does Git keep inside the .git folder?
outline: Every commit: a snapshot of the files plus its message and parent.
Branch and tag names that point at commits.

questions.text: Why does Git have a staging area between editing and committing?
outline: You choose exactly which changes go into the next commit.
Unrelated edits can wait for their own commit.
git diff --staged shows what will be saved.

questions.text: What actually happens when you create a branch?
outline: Git writes a new name pointing at the current commit; nothing is copied.
HEAD says which branch new commits move.
Switching branches swaps the files to that commit.

questions.text: Walk through resolving a merge conflict.
outline: git status lists the conflicted files.
Edit each file between the markers to the version you want.
git add the files, then git commit to finish the merge.

questions.text: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
outline: fetch downloads new commits and updates origin/* names only.
pull is fetch followed by a merge (or rebase) into your branch.
fetch first when you want to look before you merge.

questions.text: A bad commit is already pushed. How do you undo it?
outline: git revert <commit> makes a new commit that undoes it.
Push the revert like any other commit.
Avoid reset on shared branches: it rewrites history others already have.
